presentingComplaint: Brought in by ambulance drowsy and struggling to breathe after a rapidly worsening asthma attack over the preceding 3 hours.
history: 24-year-old woman with a long-standing history of poorly controlled asthma (two prior ICU admissions for near-fatal attacks, one requiring intubation). She has a history of brittle asthma with rapid symptom escalation and known reduced perception of dyspnea. She ran out of her inhaled corticosteroid/formoterol maintenance inhaler two weeks ago and has been using only an over-the-counter salbutamol inhaler intermittently. Over the last 24 hours she developed a viral upper respiratory illness with cough and today acutely worsened, using her entire salbutamol inhaler in under an hour without relief. Family noted she became confused and unusually quiet just before calling the ambulance. No known anaphylaxis trigger, no recent NSAID or beta-blocker use. Non-smoker.
examination: Drowsy, rousable only to voice, unable to complete single words. Using accessory muscles of respiration with paradoxical abdominal movement and visible tracheal tug. Central cyanosis present. On auscultation the chest is strikingly quiet with markedly reduced air entry bilaterally and only faint wheeze audible at the apices — a silent chest. Pulse is thready and rapid; pulsus paradoxus could not be reliably assessed given severity. No urticaria, angioedema, or stridor. Trachea central, no evidence of pneumothorax on exam (no tracheal deviation, equal but markedly reduced breath sounds bilaterally).
imaging: Portable chest X-ray: hyperinflated lung fields, no consolidation, no pneumothorax, no pneumomediastinum
differentialDiagnoses: Near-fatal (life-threatening) acute severe asthma with silent chest and impending respiratory arrest
Acute exacerbation of COPD (less likely given age and history)
finalDiagnosis: Near-fatal acute asthma exacerbation with silent chest, hypercapnic respiratory failure, and impending respiratory arrest

contraindications: Avoid sedatives/opioids — will worsen respiratory drive and precipitate arrest
Avoid beta-blockers (including ophthalmic) — risk of bronchospasm
Non-selective NSAIDs if history of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
Do not delay intubation in a patient with silent chest, exhaustion, and rising CO2 awaiting further trials of nebulized therapy
edgeCases: Silent chest is an ominous sign reflecting near-total airflow obstruction, not clinical improvement — wheeze intensity does not correlate with severity
Normal or rising PaCO2 in an asthmatic with tachypnea signals fatigue and impending respiratory arrest, not stabilization
Bradycardia, drowsiness, or a silent chest are life-threatening features mandating immediate ICU/anesthesia involvement and consideration of intubation
Hypokalemia is common and worsened by high-dose beta-agonist and steroid therapy — monitor potassium
